chef_bio.background: Kurumiya is a small, family-run okonomiyaki house tucked on the second floor of a building down a side street in Hiroshima's Hatchobori district, a short walk from the Tatemachi tram stop. With only about a dozen seats around a counter and a couple of tables, it has the feel of a neighborhood spot rather than a tourist destination.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop puts its pride in ingredients, using free-range (yusei-ran) eggs and its own green onions, and in a careful steaming-and-griddling technique that brings out the natural sweetness of the cabbage.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki cooked layer by layer on the griddle, with a signature 'special' piling pork, egg, squid, shrimp and noodles together; regulars order the niku-tama soba (pork-and-egg with noodles) and pile on the generous green-onion topping.

anecdotes.text: The kitchen makes a point of using free-range eggs and homemade green onions, and is known for a steaming technique that draws out the sweetness of the cabbage.
The okonomiyaki 'special' brings together meat, egg, squid, shrimp and noodles in one layered Hiroshima-style pancake.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The single griddle is used for pork, egg and seafood, so any vegetable-only order would share a surface with animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny neighborhood okonomiyaki counter where a few friendly words of Japanese and pointing at the griddle go a long way; an English menu has been noted, so a foreign student can manage comfortably.

chef_bio.background: A small teppanyaki counter-and-table spot tucked into the Nagarekawa nightlife quarter of central Hiroshima, operating since 2009. It was conceived as a place where you can taste 'all the best of Hiroshima in one spot' — pairing the city's signature ingredients with hot-griddle cooking in a relaxed setting suited to casual nights out, light entertaining, and travelers.
chef_bio.philosophy: The house keeps three words at its heart: 安心・丁寧・笑顔 — reassurance, care, and a smile. The name 一娯一笑 plays on 'one enjoyment, one smile.'
chef_bio.specialty: Premium Hiroshima oysters served both raw and grilled on the teppan — including prized 'Kanawa' brand raw oysters by the shell and grilled oysters finished with butter-soy or ponzu — alongside uni-and-spinach (uni houren) eaten with baguette, local conger eel, Hiroshima beef, and Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki.

anecdotes.text: The kitchen highlights 'Kanawa' oysters, described as among the safest, highest-quality oysters in Hiroshima, sourced from the clear Seto Inland Sea and sold by the individual shell, with a summer seasonal oyster also offered.
A signature uni-and-spinach dish is bound in the house's own mellow sea-urchin sauce and eaten with baguette — presented as a teppanyaki-style Hiroshima specialty.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Cooking is done on a shared teppan griddle, and Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki (wheat batter plus noodles) is cooked on the same surface as other dishes, making gluten cross-contact likely.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Grilled oysters are finished with butter-soy sauce or ponzu, and teppanyaki dishes use soy-based seasonings; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The menu centers on oysters, sea urchin, conger eel, and Hiroshima beef cooked on a shared griddle with butter and soy seasonings; no plant-based or vegan options are documented.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a small late-night local teppanyaki and oyster spot where some Japanese will help a lot; reservations are recommended, the room allows smoking throughout, and minors are not admitted.

The interior is often noted as refined and cafe-like, and the room tends to be calmer than the busier shops along the main approach street.

chef_bio.background: Kitchenette is the sister cafe to R[a:r] cafe, and its name means 'small kitchen.' It was conceived as an open, light-filled space inspired by the cafes of Portland, Oregon — a city admired as a place creators from around the world aspire to. The interior was designed by Makoto Tanijiri of Suppose Design Office, the Hiroshima-based architecture studio.
chef_bio.philosophy: The cafe embraces a local-production, local-consumption (地産地消) ethos and aims to be a crossroads where people meet and a platform from which Hiroshima's culture can reach the wider world.
chef_bio.specialty: The fluffy-and-runny omurice built on nutritious 15-grain rice is the signature dish, alongside a hand-formed demi-glace hamburger plate and a grass-fed-beef bagel. Cooking leans health-forward: naturally leavened bread, locally produced Sunatani milk and seasonal Hiroshima vegetables.

anecdotes.text: The cafe brews its signature 'famous-water' drip coffee with naturally alkaline 'beauty-bath' spring water sourced from the Kanagi area of Hamada, Shimane Prefecture.
The coffee program centers on Q-grade specialty beans (origins such as Brazil, Ethiopia and Costa Rica) served as hand drip.

positives.text: All cakes are made without wheat flour, offered as a gluten-free sweet option for health-conscious guests.
Health-forward sourcing: grass-fed butter, naturally leavened bread, local Sunatani-dairy milk and seasonal Hiroshima vegetables.
positives.why: 'grass-fed butter' is a misread of grass-fed beef — the page has no butter claim at all. Fix to 'grass-fed beef'. The other three elements check out.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, stylish cafe in central Hiroshima where a foreign student can order comfortably with a few Japanese words and gestures; a picture menu and well-known dishes like omurice make ordering easy, though staff may have limited English.

chef_bio.background: A neighborhood okonomiyaki shop in the Minamimachi (皆実町) district that opened in 1989 and has been run, for more than three decades, by its founder Hirano-san, who cooks alone behind the counter. Warm and talkative, she has become as much of a draw as the food, and the shop has the easy, lived-in feel of a true local institution.
chef_bio.philosophy: Her stated outlook is simple: as long as customers enjoy eating it, that's enough for her. She cooks without added oil, relying on the rendered fat from quality Hiroshima (Sera) pork, and uses firm noodles chosen to keep the dish from turning soggy, aiming for something filling yet light.
chef_bio.specialty: The house signature is 'soba rice' (そばライス): a hearty okonomiyaki layered with plenty of cabbage, pork, egg and yakisoba noodles, with sauce-coated rice folded in. It was born in the early years when a hungry high-school boy told her the standard size 'won't fill me up,' prompting her to build a more filling version that became the shop's defining dish.

anecdotes.text: The signature 'soba rice' was created after a hungry local high-school student complained that the regular okonomiyaki wouldn't fill him up, so the owner devised a bigger, rice-loaded version.

With the football powerhouse Hiroshima Minami High School nearby, the shop draws many students, and over the years athletes connected through sport — including players from Sanfrecce Hiroshima, the Hiroshima Carp, and the Hiroshima Dragonflies basketball team — have become regulars, making it a quiet hangout for local sports figures.
The owner cooks using no added oil, drawing only on the fat rendered from quality pork raised in Sera, Hiroshima, and selects firm noodles so the dish stays light rather than greasy or soggy.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki is cooked on a shared teppan griddle and built from wheat batter and wheat yakisoba noodles, so the cooking surface is heavily exposed to gluten; no gluten-free handling is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dishes are cooked using rendered pork fat on a shared griddle and center on pork and egg, so all items have animal-product contact.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, warm neighborhood counter shop run single-handedly by a chatty local owner; little to no English is likely, so a few words of Japanese and pointing at the menu will go a long way for a foreign student.

anecdotes.text: The walls are covered with autographs and signed photos from many celebrities and Hiroshima Carp players who have eaten here over the years, giving the small dining room a cluttered, well-loved feel.

The shop has been picked up as a notable Hiroshima okonomiyaki spot in voice actress Nobuyo Oyama's national restaurant-tour feature '(全国)おいしい店めぐり', helping build its reputation among visitors to the Peace Park area.

chef_bio.background: Sasa occupies a roughly 70-year-old building dating to Hiroshima's post-war reconstruction. Rather than tear it down, the owners renovated it, keeping the original brick-walled, nostalgic character so that diners step into a space that feels removed from the everyday while remaining warm and comfortable.
chef_bio.philosophy: Let the fire and the season lead: source local, fresh ingredients from the Seto Inland Sea and adjust the offering with the seasons, cooking simply at the counter hearth so guests can watch, hear, and smell the food as it cooks.
chef_bio.specialty: Robata hearth cooking using four distinct fire techniques — straw-flame searing (wara-yaki), primitive open-fire grilling (genshi-yaki), wood-fired cooking (maki-yaki), and charcoal grilling (sumibi) — applied to fresh Seto Inland Sea fish, Hiroshima oysters, local vegetables, and charcoal-grilled wagyu. Straw-seared sashimi is a signature.

anecdotes.text: The dining room is built around an irori hearth and a stone/wood-fired kiln at the counter, where guests can watch the flames and catch the aroma of food cooking over straw and charcoal.
The restaurant opened on June 1, 2020 inside a vintage 1940s-50s reconstruction-era building reworked into a brick-walled, nostalgic space.

chef_bio.background: The shop began in June 2021 as 「旬菜マルシェやました」, a direct-sales outlet for vegetables from the owner's home town of Iinan-cho in Shimane, and in September 2025 it was reborn as a sit-down obanzai lunch spot run by a husband-and-wife pair with one additional woman on staff. The cook, Yumi, holds a food-education (shokuiku) instructor qualification and still drives back to Iinan-cho two or three times a week to hand-pick seasonal vegetables, rice and other produce from a circle of local farmers.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owners want guests to feel as if they have come home to a relative's house in the countryside, and they cook with additive-free, health-minded seasonings (cane/unrefined sugar, natural sea salt, rice-bran oil) so people can eat with peace of mind.
chef_bio.specialty: A single daily 「ゆみちゃんのおばんざいランチ」 (¥1,800) — a tray of ten-plus small home-style dishes that change every day, built around Shimane vegetables, locally milled rice, and house-made seasonings like mayonnaise and sesame dressing.

anecdotes.text: The owner drives to her home town of Iinan-cho in Shimane two or three times a week to personally choose the day's vegetables from local farmers.
On the menu philosophy the cook explains she wants customers to be able to enjoy many different things, each in small portions, all at once.
The name was chosen to evoke the feeling of returning to a rural relative's home, and the kitchen deliberately uses additive-free seasonings so guests can dine safely.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The shop's own site (shunmaru831) and tabiiro confirm the June-2021 origin as vegetable direct-sales 旬菜マルシェやました and the Sept-2025 relaunch as obanzai lunch, owner/cook ゆみちゃん (shokuiku instructor) sourcing Iinan-cho (Shimane) produce 2-3 days a week, and a 10+-small-dish daily tray. A press search confirms the 3-person team (owner couple + one woman). Wink details ¥1,800 lunch, house-made mayo/sesame dressing, unrefined sugar/sea salt/rice-bran oil.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Okonomimura's official 3F floor page and corroborating listings confirm Ron on the 3rd floor of Okonomimura (中区新天地5-13), an English-speaking owner named Ron who is Hiroshima-born and opened the shop to fulfill a childhood love of okonomiyaki, with niku-tama-soba the recommended dish and cheese-mochi grilled okonomiyaki popular; the shop draws many overseas visitors.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Okonomiyaki is cooked on a shared teppan griddle alongside wheat batter and soba noodles, so cross-contact with gluten is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Hiroshima okonomiyaki is finished with a sweet okonomiyaki/Worcestershire-style sauce that is wheat- and soy-based; no gluten-free sauce is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The single shared griddle cooks pork, egg and seafood-derived items, so any dish will have animal-product cross-contact.

cultural_comfort.note: The owner, known as Ron, speaks English and is used to welcoming foreign visitors, so an exchange student can order and chat comfortably at the counter.

hiro_kaeruttei.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki is built on a wheat-flour batter/crepe and layered with wheat noodles (soba/udon), and the finishing okonomiyaki sauce typically contains wheat-derived ingredients. Squid tempura (ika-ten) topping is also wheat-battered. There is no documented gluten-free menu, dedicated fryer, or allergy accommodation.
hiro_kaeruttei.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. Dishes are cooked on a shared griddle and the standard build includes egg and pork, with toppings such as Hiroshima oysters (with bacon), scallop, squid, shrimp, and tuna-mayo; okonomiyaki/teppanyaki sauces commonly contain fish/bonito and wheat-soy. No documented vegan options.
hiro_kaeruttei.hours_raw: Mon–Sat & holidays: 11:30–24:00; Sun: 11:30–15:00. (If a Monday is a public holiday, the shop stays open Sunday and closes Monday instead.) Note: Tabelog lists Sunday as closed except for reservations, while HotPepper lists Sunday 11:30–15:00 — hours are somewhat irregular and worth confirming by phone.
hiro_kaeruttei.notes: [Mom & Pop] Kaeruttei has run its single griddle counter inside Okonomimura — the original multi-shop okonomiyaki hall in central Hiroshima — since 1991, operated by the owner with one other staff member.

chef_bio.origin: Hiroshima, in the Okonomimura building at Shintenchi.
chef_bio.background: Kaeruttei has run its single griddle counter inside Okonomimura — the original multi-shop okonomiyaki hall in central Hiroshima — since 1991, operated by the owner with one other (female) staff member across about 17 seats.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop leans toward lightly-seasoned cooking and good-quality, largely domestic and local ingredients (noodles included), with about half its customers being regulars.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki cooked in front of you on the iron plate, featuring the local touches of squid tempura and thin bean sprouts, plus seafood toppings like fresh Hiroshima oysters and scallop-butter.

anecdotes.text: The name comes from the owner's wish that customers will come back again — a play on the Japanese verb kaeru, 'to return home.'

A visitor described picking the shop on a whim inside Okonomimura and watching the okonomiyaki — with its squid tempura and thin bean sprouts, alongside oysters — cooked right in front of them on the big iron griddle, calling the result delicious.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: HotPepper explains the name (customers 'returning home', kaeru) and notes light seasoning, a commitment to main ingredients including noodles, and ~half regulars. Tabelog gives opening year 1991, 17 seats, a two-person owner+one-female-staff operation inside Okonomimura, and toppings of squid tempura, bean sprouts and scallop-butter. A note.com visitor confirms squid tempura, thin bean sprouts and oysters grilled at the counter.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Okonomiyaki is made on a shared iron griddle with wheat-flour batter and wheat noodles, so heavy gluten cross-contact is unavoidable in this style of cooking.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All dishes are cooked together on one communal griddle alongside pork, egg, and seafood, so plant-only preparation cannot be assured.

positives.text: Ingredients are largely domestic/local and the cooking is described as lightly seasoned, and the food is prepared on the griddle in front of you so you can see exactly what goes in.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny owner-run griddle counter inside the Okonomimura okonomiyaki hall with about half regulars; a little Japanese helps, but pointing at menu items and watching the chef cook on the iron plate in front of you makes ordering manageable.

hiro_shimai.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The core dish is Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki, which is built on a wheat-flour crepe batter and layered with wheat noodles (soba/udon), and finished with okonomiyaki sauce (Otafuku-style) that contains wheat. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented.
hiro_shimai.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki here is standardly made with egg, pork, and seafood, and uses bonito/fish-based elements and wheat-soy okonomiyaki sauce. No vegan options are documented.
hiro_shimai.notes: [Mom & Pop] 姉妹 is one of the small okonomiyaki stalls inside お好み共和国ひろしま村, a Shintenchi food complex devoted to Hiroshima's post-war okonomiyaki culture. chef_bio.background: 姉妹 is one of the small okonomiyaki stalls inside お好み共和国ひろしま村, a Shintenchi food complex devoted to Hiroshima's post-war okonomiyaki culture. The shop is known for a former sumo wrestler who works the teppan, grilling each Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki by hand in full view of the counter.
chef_bio.philosophy: The building it sits in espouses okonomiyaki that evokes nostalgia without heavy seasoning, rooted in Hiroshima's postwar food culture.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki — the layered, wheat-crepe-and-noodle griddle dish that the surrounding complex is built around.

anecdotes.text: The cook at the griddle is a former sumo wrestler, and customers come to watch him grill the okonomiyaki right in front of them at the counter.
The shop sits inside お好み共和国ひろしま村, a Shintenchi okonomiyaki complex focused on unfussy, nostalgic Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The complex's official shoplist places 姉妹 inside お好み共和国ひろしま村 in Shintenchi (Naka-ku), a themed hall of postwar-style Hiroshima okonomiyaki. Tabelog/gnavi listings and search results confirm the stall is run by a former sumo wrestler (with a sumo-stable training connection), ~16 seats on the 2F, open daily. No published personal name for the cook was found, so chef_name is left null.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 7-seat counter okonomiyaki stall inside a multi-shop building, where you watch the cook work the griddle right in front of you — a few words of Japanese and a smile go a long way, and pointing at what others are eating works fine.

hiro_shirunashi_tantanmen_sen_3.gf_detail: The signature dish is wheat-noodle dandan noodles, and the savory tare typically relies on soy sauce (which contains wheat) plus meat- and sesame-based seasonings. There is no documented gluten-free option, so this is not suitable for gluten-free or celiac diners.
hiro_shirunashi_tantanmen_sen_3.vegan_detail: This is a meat-forward noodle shop — the dandan noodles and the other recommended bowls (chicken soba) are built on chicken/pork umami and animal-based broths and toppings. No vegan option is documented.
hiro_shirunashi_tantanmen_sen_3.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small specialist shop devoted to shirunashi tantanmen — Hiroshima-style brothless dandan noodles — that opened on September 29, 2014. It sits a one- to two-minute walk from the Hiroden Tsuchihashi tram stop in the Koamicho district just west of the Peace Memorial Park

chef_bio.origin: Hiroshima, central Naka Ward near Tsuchihashi/Dobashi
chef_bio.background: A small specialist shop devoted to shirunashi tantanmen — Hiroshima-style brothless dandan noodles — that opened on September 29, 2014. It sits a one- to two-minute walk from the Hiroden Tsuchihashi tram stop in the Koamicho district (小網町7-1) just west of the Peace Memorial Park, and runs as a compact 12-seat counter operation.
chef_bio.philosophy: Build the bowl on layered texture and umami: a chicken-bone-based tare, chewy noodles, generous pickled mustard greens (zaasai), and crunchy garlic chips.
chef_bio.specialty: Brothless dandan noodles (汁なし担々麺) served at 800 yen, with the eater choosing both a spice level (0, 1, 2, 3, or MAX) and a temperature (hot or cold); a chicken soba and a jiro-style bowl have since been added.

anecdotes.text: A distinctive feature of the bowl is the unusual sweetness of the pickled mustard greens (zaasai), which gives the dish more richness and depth than a typical brothless dandan noodle.
Regulars treat a small portion of rice as essential to soak up the seasoned sauce left at the bottom of the bowl, and table-side garlic-chip chili oil lets you shift the flavor partway through.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog gives the opening date 2014.9.29, 12 counter seats, and a tare built on chicken-bone broth (鶏ガラ) with red miso, sugar and dark soy. Modokimaru confirms the ¥800 price, spice levels 0/1/2/3/MAX, hot-or-cold choice, address 小網町7-1, crunchy zaasai, table garlic-chip chili oil, and rice to soak the sauce. Pokomichi highlights the signature sweetness of the zaasai and notes a later change of ownership that added chicken soba and jiro-style ramen.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Single-counter shop centered entirely on wheat noodles, so gluten is present throughout the cooking line; no gluten-free handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The savory tare for brothless dandan noodles characteristically uses soy sauce, which contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All featured dishes use chicken/pork umami and animal toppings; a shared single-counter kitchen means no separation from animal ingredients.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 12-seat counter shop run single-handedly with a ticket-machine ordering system, so a little Japanese (or pointing at the menu) helps; just pick your spice level (0 to MAX) and hot or cold.

hiro_chugoku_ryori_kawanami.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodation indicated. The signature dishes are wheat-noodle tantanmen and brothless tantanmen, and Sichuan stir-fries here use soy sauce and likely wheat-based seasonings. No dedicated GF menu or preparation is documented, so this is not suitable for someone requiring strict gluten avoidance.
hiro_chugoku_ryori_kawanami.vegan_detail: Not vegan-oriented. The menu centers on meat-based Sichuan dishes (mapo tofu typically with pork, karaage, beef oyster-sauce stir-fry) and pork/sesame-based tantanmen. No documented vegan options or plant-based preparation. Vegetable dishes likely contain meat-derived stocks, soy sauce, or oyster sauce.
hiro_chugoku_ryori_kawanami.notes: The owner-chef built his craft over a long apprenticeship in authentic Sichuan cooking before opening this small restaurant a short walk from Hiroshima Station, where he turns out classic Sichuan dishes alongside the city's beloved brothless tantanmen.

chef_bio.background: The owner-chef built his craft over a long apprenticeship in authentic Sichuan cooking before opening this small restaurant a short walk from Hiroshima Station, where he turns out classic Sichuan dishes alongside the city's beloved brothless tantanmen.
chef_bio.philosophy: Bringing genuine Sichuan technique to an everyday neighborhood setting, and giving the local brothless tantanmen a personal twist with added vegetables.
chef_bio.specialty: Brothless tantanmen (shirunashi tantanmen) and Sichuan classics such as mapo tofu

anecdotes.text: The owner-chef is described as having trained for 21 years under celebrated Sichuan master Chen Kenichi at Shisen Hanten, grounding the kitchen in serious Sichuan technique.
His brothless tantanmen stands out by including bean sprouts, where most Hiroshima versions use only green onion as a topping, adding a fresh vegetable element to the dish.
It is cited as one of the closest places to Hiroshima Station's Shinkansen exit to get a proper bowl of brothless tantanmen, about a 5-7 minute walk away.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Umaihiroshima reports the owner-chef trained 21 years under Chen Kenichi (陳建一) at Shisen Hanten (四川飯店), that his brothless tantanmen uniquely adds bean sprouts (where most Hiroshima shops use only green onion), and that the shop is about a 5-minute walk from Hiroshima Station's Shinkansen exit — one of the closest spots for a proper bowl; the ¥800 set includes rice and almond tofu, and mapo tofu is on the menu.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The brothless tantanmen is described as having a soy-sauce-based seasoning, and Japanese soy sauce is typically brewed with wheat.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, casual neighborhood Chinese restaurant where a few words of Japanese and pointing at the menu will get you a warm welcome and a great bowl of noodles.

hiro_yamadaya_miyajima_honten.gf_detail: Their signature momiji manju and kiriyoka are wheat-flour confections (castella-style sponge), so the core products are not gluten-free. No gluten-free menu or dedicated allergen handling is documented.
hiro_yamadaya_miyajima_honten.vegan_detail: Momiji manju is a castella-batter cake that traditionally contains eggs (and commonly dairy/honey in modern varieties), so it is not vegan. No vegan products or labeling are documented for this shop.
hiro_yamadaya_miyajima_honten.hours_raw: 9:00–18:00; open daily (both the shop and cafe)
hiro_yamadaya_miyajima_honten.notes: [Miyajima] Yamadaya is a long-established Miyajima confectioner founded in 1932 as a maker of momiji manju, the maple-leaf-shaped cakes that are the island's signature sweet. Its main store sits along the busy approach to Itsukushima Shrine. (Map pin approximate — Omotesandō; use the Maps link for exact spot.)

chef_bio.background: Yamadaya is a long-established Miyajima confectioner founded in 1932 (Showa 7) as a maker of momiji manju, the maple-leaf-shaped cakes that are the island's signature sweet. Its main store sits on Miyajima (宮島町835-1), along the approach to Itsukushima Shrine.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop emphasizes that its confections are all handmade by artisans, and at the main store visitors can watch the sweets being made and even hand-bake their own.
chef_bio.specialty: Momiji manju in a wide range of flavors (more than a dozen year-round, over twenty including seasonal varieties) and its own popular kiriyoka (桐葉菓) — a chewy mochi-flour cake filled with a blend of house-made smooth and chunky bean paste, the shop's number-one seller.

anecdotes.text: The Miyajima main store doubles as an experience destination: a corner offers hand-baking of momiji manju (by reservation, with a souvenir), and an attached cafe (RAKU山田屋) serves the brand's handmade sweets on site.
Yamadaya developed kiriyoka, a chewy chestnut-brown mochi cake of blended bean pastes, which has become the brand's number-one product alongside momiji manju.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Yamadaya's official site and company profile give a founding of 1932 (昭和7年10月20日), 13+ year-round momiji-manju flavors (20+ with seasonal ones), and kiriyoka (桐葉菓) — mochi-flour wrapped around blended smooth/chunky bean paste — as the top seller, all handmade by artisans. The store page confirms the Miyajima main shop (宮島町835-1), hand-baking corner/experience and the RAKU山田屋 handmade-sweets cafe.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Signature products (momiji manju, kiriyoka) are wheat-flour cakes made in a shared confectionery production environment; no gluten-free handling is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Momiji manju is an egg-based castella cake; no vegan products or egg/dairy-free handling are documented.

hiro_taishu_shokudo_yunosuke.gf_detail: Not gluten-free friendly. The kitchen is built around wheat-based soy sauce, fried foods and dumpling-style items like shumai, so gluten is pervasive and there is no documented gluten-free option or allergy handling. Celiac and gluten-sensitive diners should avoid.
hiro_taishu_shokudo_yunosuke.vegan_detail: No vegan offering is documented. This is a meat-and-fish-forward town-Chinese shokudo and izakaya (shumai, fried dishes, set meals with soup, pickles and salad). Dishes are built around pork and other meats and are seasoned with soy-sauce-based seasonings; no plant-based menu or vegan accommodation has been described.
hiro_taishu_shokudo_yunosuke.hours_raw: Mon, Wed-Sat 17:00-23:00 (L.O. 22:30); Sun 11:30-23:00 (L.O. 22:30); Tue closed. (Some sources list weekday lunch service 11:30-15:00; hours appear to vary, so confirm before a daytime visit.)
hiro_taishu_shokudo_yunosuke.notes: Opened on April 25, 2023, this is a modern take on the old-school neighborhood Chinese diner, billed as a town-Chinese (machi-chuka) eatery crossed with a neo-izakaya. chef_bio.origin: Hiroshima, in the Hondori arcade district of central Naka-ku.
chef_bio.background: Opened on April 25, 2023, this is a modern take on the old-school neighborhood Chinese diner, billed as a town-Chinese (machi-chuka) eatery crossed with a neo-izakaya. It is the kind of place built for everything from a midday set meal to an early, casual drink with friends.
chef_bio.philosophy: An easygoing, anyone-welcome shokudo atmosphere where you can eat well and drink casually from daytime onward.
chef_bio.specialty: Hearty daily set meals and town-Chinese standards that rotate regularly, with the meat shumai set a signature plate; portions are known for being generous.

anecdotes.text: The shop has a retro bathhouse-tile look outside with white square tiles and a white noren curtain, and inside, cream walls, a wooden counter and a big TV for catching baseball games.
The signature meat shumai set (about 900 yen) comes with rice, soup, pickles and salad; the shumai has a dense, slightly chewy texture and arrives fast and piping hot.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Modokimaru and listing sites confirm 遊のすけ opened 2023-04-25 as a 町中華×ネオ居酒屋 at 中区本通1-22 (33 seats), serving from lunch with alcohol available from daytime; the exterior uses white square bathhouse-style tiles and a white noren, and the signature 肉しゅうまい set is ¥900 with rice, soup, pickles and salad. A specific '~21' set-meal count could not be verified, so it is described as a regularly rotating lineup.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Menu centers on fried town-Chinese dishes, dumplings/shumai and soy-sauce-seasoned plates, so wheat and shared frying are expected throughout the kitchen.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Town-Chinese set meals and izakaya dishes are seasoned with standard Japanese/Chinese soy-sauce-based seasonings, which contain wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dishes are meat- and fish-forward (pork shumai, set meals with soup); no plant-based or vegan preparation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, welcoming local eatery where a foreign student will be comfortable, though menus and staff are mostly in Japanese, so a translation app or pointing at dishes helps.

hiro_chuka_soba_tsubame.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The core dish is Chinese-style wheat ramen noodles in a pork-bone soy-sauce broth; the soy sauce contains wheat. The oden is simmered in the same soy-based ramen stock and includes wheat-containing items (fish cakes, etc.). There is no documented gluten-free menu or accommodation.
hiro_chuka_soba_tsubame.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The signature broth is a long-simmered pork-bone (tonkotsu) soy-sauce base, topped with house chashu (pork) and the oden is built on the same animal stock. No documented vegan or vegetarian options.
hiro_chuka_soba_tsubame.hours_raw: Mon–Sat 11:30-22:00 (L.O. 21:40-21:50); closed Sun. Closed for New Year (Dec 31–Jan 4).
hiro_chuka_soba_tsubame.notes: [Mom & Pop] A family-run Hiroshima ramen shop that has been serving the same pork-bone, soy-sauce-based chuka soba for around 40 years. The business has carried on across three generations, with the previous-generation owner still involved in preparing the broth, keeping the recipe

chef_bio.origin: Hiroshima, started as a street-stall (yatai) ramen operation
chef_bio.background: A family-run Hiroshima ramen shop that has been serving the same pork-bone, soy-sauce-based chuka soba for around 40 years. The business has carried on across three generations, with the previous-generation owner still involved in preparing the broth, keeping the recipe and methods unchanged from the shop's street-stall beginnings.
chef_bio.philosophy: A commitment to keeping the time-honored taste consistent rather than chasing trends - just the same broth done carefully, with a welcoming neighborhood atmosphere.
chef_bio.specialty: Classic Hiroshima-style chuka soba: a pork-bone and soy-sauce broth with house-made chashu, green onion, and bean sprouts. Alongside the ramen, the shop simmers oden in a stock based on the same ramen broth, offering about eight varieties; the daikon radish is a standout, made by sourcing large radishes and using only the center portions, simmered for a precise time.

anecdotes.text: The pork-bone soy-sauce broth has been kept unchanged for about 40 years, passed down across three generations, with the former owner still helping make the soup today.
The oden is built on the ramen's own soup stock; the daikon is prepared from large radishes using only the center sections, simmered for a precise duration for the best flavor.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The shop's own gorp page states the pork-bone soy-sauce broth has stayed unchanged ~40 years across three generations with the previous owner still making it, traces the business to a yatai street stall, and lists chashu/green onion/bean sprouts on the chuka soba. It also describes oden built on the ramen stock (8 kinds, ~¥150 each), with the prized daikon cut only from the centers of large radishes and simmered a precise time. Seating is ~7 tables + 3 counter.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles and a wheat-containing soy-sauce broth are central to the menu, and oden shares the same soy-based stock, so gluten is pervasive throughout the kitchen.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is a soy-sauce (shoyu) base, which in standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is pork-bone based with pork chashu, and oden uses the same animal stock and fish-based items, so no dishes are free of animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a no-frills, cash-only local ramen counter where ordering is in Japanese; a foreign student comfortable pointing at the menu and knowing a few basic phrases will do fine, but little to no English support should be expected.

hiro_blue_mountain.gf_detail: No gluten-free offering is documented. This is a traditional kissaten whose menu centers on omelette rice (omurice), hamburger steak, cakes and morning toast sets — wheat-based dishes and bread dominate, and there is no evidence of any gluten-free preparation or awareness. Celiac travelers should treat it as unsuitable.
hiro_blue_mountain.vegan_detail: No vegan options are documented. Signature dishes (omurice made with egg, hamburger steak with demi-glace, cake sets, morning sets with toast and egg) rely on egg, dairy and meat. There is no evidence of plant-based menu items, so vegans should treat it as unsuitable.
hiro_blue_mountain.notes: [Mom & Pop] A long-running retro coffee shop tucked on the second floor of a building along the bustling Hondori shopping arcade in central Hiroshima, said to date back several decades. It is the kind of nostalgic neighborhood kissaten where regulars gather for conversation away fr

chef_bio.background: A long-running retro coffee shop tucked on the second floor of a building along the bustling Hondori shopping arcade in central Hiroshima. It is the kind of nostalgic neighborhood kissaten where regulars gather for conversation away from the crowds of the street below.
chef_bio.specialty: Old-fashioned coffee-shop fare, with omelette rice (omurice) — a fluffy egg over shrimp-and-pepper fried rice, topped with a small hamburger steak and sauce (¥1,200) — as a signature plate, alongside a morning toast set and cake/curry options.

anecdotes.text: The interior leans into Showa-era nostalgia: cream-toned walls and ceilings hung with artwork, red velvet chairs and chandelier-style lighting, with fresh flowers set on the tables.
Tables are finished with thin wooden strips about 5mm thick that give a subtle texture, and the upstairs room stays quiet and relaxed despite sitting right above the busy arcade.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog describes ブルーマウンテン as a 2F retro kissaten on Hondori with cream ceilings, wall artwork, wood flooring, red velvet chairs and chandelier lighting (26 seats), serving morning toast sets, omurice, curry and mini-cakes, with an omurice-with-hamburger plate at ¥1,200. Oomin's blog confirms the 2F-above-the-arcade quiet, table surfaces of ~5mm wooden strips, fresh flowers, and the omurice topped with a small hamburger and sauce. No source states a specific founding year.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, regulars-oriented retro coffee shop with no indication of English support, so a foreign student is best off going with a Japanese-speaking guide or being prepared to point at the menu and use simple Japanese.

hiro_setouchi_grill_zipang.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodation indicated. The kitchen centers on anago (conger eel) prepared with sweet soy-based tare and tempura items (oysters, small sardines) coated in wheat batter and deep-fried in shared oil. Standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. There is no documentation of GF menu items, GF soy sauce, or any allergen handling.
hiro_setouchi_grill_zipang.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The menu is built around seafood (Seto Inland Sea conger eel, Miyajima oysters), fish cake (gansu), pork bowls, and karaage. Sauces are soy/fish-based. No documented vegan or vegetarian dishes.

cultural_comfort.note: A neighborhood Taiwanese spot where ordering happens in Japanese; no confirmation that English is spoken, so a foreign student may want a translation app or a guide for the herbal hot pot, which can be tailored to your body and the season if you ask in advance.

chef_bio.background: Founded in 1924 (Taisho 13), Gonbei is regarded as Hiroshima's oldest oden house. It began as a kaiseki restaurant where oden was first served almost as an appetizer while diners waited for their main courses, gradually becoming the dish the place is now known for. Originally in the western entertainment quarter before the war, it moved after the atomic bombing and settled in the Nagarekawa/Yakenbori nightlife district in 1953. The shop is now run by Kodama, the fourth-generation proprietor.
chef_bio.philosophy: The house links its miso oden to the older tradition of dengaku (田楽), historically served with miso: the founder chose Fuchu white miso because it most closely resembled the miso he had used during his apprenticeship in Kyoto, blending it with the house dashi to create the restaurant's distinctive sauce.
chef_bio.specialty: Two styles of oden: a Seto Inland Sea dashi oden and a signature white-miso oden made with Fuchu miso, including local oysters and anago (conger eel). A range of handmade items and unusual ingredients also appear, and meals are often finished with chameshi (tea rice), optionally with miso.

anecdotes.text: The unusual name is said to come from the old phrase 'nanashi no Gonbei' (nameless Gonbei): the shop operated without an official name, so people simply called it Gonbei - though the source notes this is an unconfirmed 'so they say' story.
The founder selected Fuchu white miso for the signature miso oden because it reminded him of the miso he had used during his apprenticeship in Kyoto.
The restaurant has kept a partnership of more than 50 years with Sapporo Lager beer.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: akaboshi-tanteidan (a Sapporo Lager interview) confirms the ~100-year history, both dashi and miso oden, the Fuchu white miso chosen because the founder trained in Kyoto (初代が京都で修行... 一番近いのが府中市のみそ), the 50-year Sapporo tie, and identifies the current owner as fourth-generation Kodama-san (大将の児玉さん / 自分で4代目) - no first name given. shinise.tv gives the 1924 founding, 1953 Yakenbori move, and the hedged 'nanashi no Gonbei' name-origin tale.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Oden simmers all ingredients together in shared fish dashi alongside oysters, anago, beef and chicken items, so vegetable items are not free of animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A historic, well-loved local oden house where Japanese is the working language and payment is cash only, so come with some basic phrases or a translation app and be ready to point at what looks good on the counter.

chef_bio.background: Suekichi is a small, owner-run oden specialist tucked into central Hiroshima. For years it occupied a cramped little space near the Kanayamacho (Ginzan-cho) tram stop before moving in May 2025 to a cleaner, calmer room of its own, carrying over its old fixtures to keep the same feel - a quiet refuge from the surrounding nightlife district.
chef_bio.philosophy: An unhurried, careful approach: a hushed, relaxed atmosphere and patiently simmered ingredients, prizing refinement over bustle.
chef_bio.specialty: A clear, gentle, Kyoto-leaning oden dashi rather than a heavy dark broth. Beyond the classics like slow-simmered daikon and soft-boiled egg, the pot features Hiroshima's local 'koune' (beef neck meat) and unusual seasonal pieces such as scallop, sea cucumber and fresh wakame.

anecdotes.text: Reviewers describe the oden as 'upper class yet rich in flavor' and 'gentle,' set in a calm, quiet room that feels subdued rather than rowdy despite sitting in the middle of the entertainment district.
In May 2025 the shop relocated from its former cramped venue to a cleaner, more accessible space, bringing over fixtures to recreate the previous ambiance.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: tabelog reviews confirm the May 8, 2025 relocation near Ginzan-cho (銀山町, romanized Kanayama-cho) station, koune/wakame/scallop/sea-cucumber oden, and a refined dashi ('上品だけどコクのある美味しいおでん'). The shop's Instagram account (@odensuekichi96) carries the owner's name 黒川 正法 (Kurokawa Masanori).

cultural_comfort.note: A quiet, intimate counter-style oden shop where ordering is easiest with some basic Japanese; phone reservations help, and pointing at the day's oden pot works if you don't speak the language.

anecdotes.text: The signature is the shiso-laced 'Jirokichi' okonomiyaki, while the most-repeated order is the 'Jirokichi roll' packing soba noodles, scallion and cheese into a crisp roll. Look for the yellow sign across from the Seven-Eleven, about a 10-minute walk from Fukuromachi tram stop.

Because traditional okonomiyaki uses egg and meat that vegans and vegetarians cannot eat, the shop makes a point of offering vegetarian and vegan versions plus gluten-free accommodation, and is noted as very popular with overseas visitors.

Effectively fully plant-based: multiple reviews state it uses no meat, fish, or eggs, and it operates as shojin (Buddhist temple) style Chinese cuisine. chef_bio.background: 桂愛 (Keiai) opened on April 14, 2024 in a previously vacant storefront in Nakamachi, central Hiroshima (Churis Nakamachi Bldg 1F), and is run by two women, one cooking and one handling the front of house.
chef_bio.philosophy: Cooking based on Buddhist temple cuisine (精進料理) that uses no meat, fish, or eggs and also omits the five pungent roots (garlic, onions, scallions, Chinese chives), aiming for a gentle, compassionate flavor.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegan/vegetarian Chinese cooking in a Buddhist shojin style: soy-meat mapo tofu, soy-sauce ramen, soy-meat karaage, and gyoza, with plant-based stock and a daily lunch set around 990 yen.

anecdotes.text: Local food writers repeatedly call it possibly the only vegetarian Chinese restaurant in the city, and note that vegan/vegetarian Chinese is an unusual, almost unheard-of concept locally.
A reviewer described the soy-protein dishes as having a gently compassionate flavor (じんわりと慈悲深い味), lighter than meat-based versions.
Another diner emphasized it serves completely vegetarian Chinese food with no meat, fish, or eggs, nor the five pungent roots.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: modokimaru confirms the April 14, 2024 opening at Churis Nakamachi Bldg 1F, the two-woman operation, shojin principles (no meat/fish/egg, no garlic/onion/scallion/nira), the ~990-yen lunch set of soy-sauce ramen, mapo tofu and karaage, the 'first vegan/vegetarian Chinese I'd heard of in the city' remark, and the 'じんわりと慈悲深い味' description. ameblo corroborates the fully vegetarian, five-pungent-free cooking.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Menu includes soy-sauce (shoyu) ramen, indicating use of regular wheat-based soy sauce typical of Chinese cooking.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Kitchen is described as entirely plant-based with no meat, fish, or eggs used anywhere, which substantially limits animal-product cross-contact risk.

positives.text: Fully plant-based shojin-style Chinese kitchen using no meat, fish, or eggs, making it a reliable choice for vegans and vegetarians.
Also omits the five pungent roots (garlic, onion, scallion, Chinese chives), helpful for those following strict shojin or allium-free diets.

cultural_comfort.note: Small two-person family-style shop with a ticket vending machine and Japanese-language menu, so basic Japanese or a translation app helps, but the all-plant menu makes ordering low-stress for a foreign student.

chef_bio.specialty: Casual French bistro cooking built around carefully sourced Hiroshima and nationwide ingredients: at lunch, a rotating range of sandwiches on house-baked bread; at dinner, proper French dishes such as oyster bourguignon (牡蠣のブルギニョン) and ayu confit (鮎のコンフィ), paired with local sake, craft beer, and sommelier-chosen wine.

Lunch centers on sandwiches pairing select ingredients with house-baked bread, while dinner offers full French dishes like oyster bourguignon and ayu confit.

positives.text: The restaurant explicitly provides a vegetarian and vegan menu in addition to its standard offerings.

cultural_comfort.note: A small chef-run bistro on Miyajima used to international tourists; lunchtime sandwiches are very approachable, and it is wise to reserve ahead online for dinner and to point to the menu rather than relying on English.

It serves Hiroshima beef sukiyaki and quietly focuses on giving each visiting group an unhurried, attentive meal, preparing the sukiyaki carefully for one party at a time.
chef_bio.philosophy: The name draws on the spirit of the historic Rokumeikan as a place where people gather, converse, and are welcomed; the kitchen sources beef, vegetables, eggs, and seasonings from Hiroshima as much as possible and aims to preserve the natural flavor of each ingredient while leaving diners with a calm memory.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima beef sukiyaki, with tiered sets (梅/竹/松, roughly 80g-240g of beef) that pair the beef with carefully selected seasonal vegetables, grilled tofu, Hiroshima egg, rice, and red miso soup.

anecdotes.text: The shop welcomes small parties and notes that reservations for even two or three guests are no problem, reflecting its intimate, one-group-at-a-time style.
It opened recently as a new sukiyaki restaurant on Miyajima, about a two-minute walk from the ferry pier.

chef_bio.background: This is the sōhonten (flagship head shop) of Chinchikurin, a Hiroshima okonomiyaki and teppan house on Yagenbori street in central Naka-ku. The shop frames itself as a keeper of Hiroshima's food culture, presenting layered Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki as the city's local soul food and welcoming solo diners, families, and regulars at its counter and tatami seats.
chef_bio.philosophy: Inheriting and advancing Hiroshima's okonomiyaki culture, with an emphasis on the shared, convivial experience between the cook at the teppan and the diner.
chef_bio.specialty: The house namesake 'Chinchikurin-yaki' is a classic Hiroshima okonomiyaki built with egg and squid tempura; other signatures include a beef-chuck (中落ち) okonomiyaki and a mentaiko-cheese version, alongside teppan-grilled offal and seafood. The noodles are custom-made by Isono Seimen and are thoroughly blanched to bring out their natural sweetness, then seared in soybean oil for a crisp-outside, chewy-inside texture, and paired with Otafuku sauce.

anecdotes.text: The kitchen sources its okonomiyaki noodles from a dedicated noodle maker, Isono Seimen, and blanches them to draw out sweetness before searing in soybean oil for a crisp-yet-chewy finish.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 公式サイト（chinchikurin.com / okonomiyaki.chinchikurin.com）が、当店を広島市中区薬研堀通りにある『ちんちくりんの総本店』とし、磯野製麺の麺をしっかり湯がいて甘みを引き出し大豆白絞油で焼き上げること、オタフクソース使用、看板のちんちくりん焼（玉子・いか天）、中落ち・明太チーズ等のメニュー、広島の食文化を受け継ぎ発展させる姿勢を明記している。

cultural_comfort.note: A lively, welcoming teppan counter where the cook interacts with diners; a few words of Japanese and pointing at the menu will go a long way, and solo diners and families are explicitly welcomed.

chef_bio.background: A small, family-run okonomiyaki and teppanyaki shop tucked into the Nobori-chō neighborhood in central Hiroshima, an easy walk from the Hondōri and Hatchōbori shopping streets. The proprietor honed the craft at a well-known Hiroshima okonomiyaki shop before striking out to open this independent counter spot.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop leans into the energy of the open counter, where guests sit close to the griddle and watch their food cooked in front of them, paired with table seats that have their own built-in teppan grills.
chef_bio.specialty: Hearty Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki where the noodles are spread wide and crisped on the griddle and dusted with garlic powder for a savory, energizing finish; signature plates include the house Mihera-yaki, a spicy tan-tan style okonomiyaki, and a crispy griddle-fried potato salad. There are also colour-coded topping sets (red kimchi/gochujang, black curry/cheese, white cream/cheese) and teppanyaki small plates like lotus-root butter grill and garlic shrimp.

anecdotes.text: The name 三箆 (Mihera) refers to three overlapping griddle spatulas (hera), which form the shop's logo.
The okonomiyaki noodles are spread wide and crisped on the teppan with lard into individual strands and finished with garlic powder for a crunchy, savory bite.

chef_bio.background: Yatsunami opened in November 2019 in the Kamihatchobori business district, a short walk from Hiroshima Castle and Shukkeien Garden (about 170m from Shukkeien-mae streetcar stop). Owner-chef Yasuo Yoshino (born 1981), who grew up in Hiroshima and discovered okonomiyaki through student part-time work, trained at well-regarded Hiroshima okonomiyaki shops and at teppanyaki restaurants in Tokyo before opening his own counter. He largely runs the place himself, cooking on the griddle in front of guests at its roughly 21 seats.
chef_bio.philosophy: Yoshino aims to preserve the 'unchanging, old-fashioned flavors of Hiroshima' (昔ながらの変わらない広島の味) and to keep the shop a relaxed gathering place for the neighborhood. He sources locally, using Isono Seimen noodles and Otafuku sauce.
chef_bio.specialty: Classic Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki layered with cabbage and crisp noodles (the signature 'Yatsunami-yaki'), alongside teppanyaki such as salt-grilled corne (rare marbled beef shoulder). The slow-simmered pork-cartilage stew (豚軟骨のすじ煮込み) in a lightly sweet broth is described as the most repeat-ordered dish.

anecdotes.text: The lightly sweet slow-cooked pork-cartilage stew is reported to be the restaurant's most repeat-ordered item.

chef_bio.background: One of the original sources of Hiroshima-style chuka soba. The shop traces back to 1948 (Showa 23), when three ramen yatai (food stalls) appeared in postwar Hiroshima and launched the city's ramen culture; Uguisu was one of those three. The founder is said to have learned how to make soup at a small eatery in Manchuria before opening a stall in Hiroshima's Nakashinjidai district, eventually settling into the Nagarekawa shop that has watched over the neighborhood's nightlife for decades.
chef_bio.specialty: Old-fashioned tonkotsu-shoyu (pork-bone soy sauce) chuka soba, often ordered with a generous heap of green onions (negi chuka soba), plus simple oden simmering on the counter as a side.

anecdotes.text: Hiroshima's ramen tradition is said to have begun in 1948 with three yatai stalls, one of which was Uguisu, making it one of the headwaters of the city's chuka soba.
The founder reportedly learned soup-making at a small restaurant in Manchuria before opening a stall in Hiroshima, later moving into the long-running Nagarekawa shop.
A cramped late-night counter that opens into the small hours (roughly 20:00-26:00) to catch the after-party crowd of the Nagarekawa entertainment district.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Pork-bone broth and chashu pork are the foundation of the dish; oden uses fish/meat dashi. No vegan preparation exists.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny late-night counter run single-handedly with a regular, mostly Japanese-speaking crowd, so basic Japanese and an easygoing attitude help; point at the menu, order chuka soba, and pay in cash.

hiro_chuka_soba_senban_nagare.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The core dish is wheat ramen noodles in a soy-sauce-based broth (Japanese soy sauce contains wheat), with sides like fried rice and gyoza. No gluten-free options or accommodations are documented.
hiro_chuka_soba_senban_nagare.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The signature broth is a soy-based pork-bone (tonkotsu) stock simmered 12+ hours, and dishes include chashu pork, pork belly, and other meat. No vegan options are documented.
hiro_chuka_soba_senban_nagare.hours_raw: Per official site: Tuesday-Saturday, holidays and days before holidays 19:00-03:00 (next day), last order 02:30; closed Mondays and Sundays, with irregular closures. (Other listings report longer/daily hours including a lunch service, so hours may vary.)
hiro_chuka_soba_senban_nagare.notes: A Hiroshima institution founded in 1951 (Showa 26) in the Nagarekawa entertainment district, this chuka soba shop has fed the city's nightlife for over 68 years. chef_bio.background: A Hiroshima institution founded in 1951 (Showa 26) in the Nagarekawa entertainment district, this chuka soba shop has fed the city's nightlife for over 68 years. The current generation carries on the recipe inherited from the founder, describing it as a taste unchanged since the previous owner's day.
chef_bio.philosophy: Preserving the founder's flavor through patient, slow cooking while making a bowl people want to eat every day.
chef_bio.specialty: Chuka soba in a soy-sauce-based broth simmered for more than 12 hours, paired with a secret tare aged for three weeks. The result is a deeply savory but not heavy bowl, distinct from Hakata or Onomichi styles. Unusually for a ramen shop, the menu also carries 20-plus generous side dishes, with the fried rice a standout.

anecdotes.text: Beloved as a spot for the post-drinking finishing bowl, it stays open into the early hours (until around 3am) to serve Nagarekawa's nightlife crowd.
The broth is simmered over 12 hours and the secret tare is aged three weeks, a recipe carried on unchanged from the founder.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 公式（owst）とホットペッパーが、昭和26年（1951年）創業・流川の老舗で創業68年、先代からの味を変えずに引き継ぐこと、12時間以上煮込むスープと3週間熟成の秘伝ダレ、20種類以上のサイドメニュー（焼きめしが人気）、深夜3時までの締めの一杯として親しまれることを伝える。

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature broth is soy-sauce-based, and Japanese soy sauce normally contains wheat; the noodles are also wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is a pork-bone (tonkotsu) and soy stock and many dishes contain pork, so vegan diners cannot be accommodated.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a late-night local ramen and izakaya spot where ordering in basic Japanese (or by pointing at the menu) is expected; little to no English is documented, so a few phrases will help.

hiro_ramen_kakimoto.gf_detail: No gluten-free options. The chuka soba is built on wheat ramen noodles and a soy-sauce-based broth (Japanese soy sauce contains wheat), and the menu centers on noodles, fried rice, and shumai (wheat wrapper). Nothing on the menu is suitable for a strict gluten-free diet.
hiro_ramen_kakimoto.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The broth is meat/soy-sauce based and the signature bowl comes with slow-cooked pork chashu; sides include karaage (fried chicken), oden, and pork shumai. No documented vegetable-only or vegan options.
hiro_ramen_kakimoto.hours_raw: Tue–Thu, Sun & holidays: 21:00–03:00 (L.O. 02:30); Fri–Sat: 21:00–05:00 (L.O. 04:30); closed Mondays.
hiro_ramen_kakimoto.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, unpretentious late-night ramen counter tucked into the Nagarekawa-Yakkenbori nightlife district of central Hiroshima, about 1.5km from the Peace Memorial Park. It draws a steady crowd of locals looking for a warming bowl to close out an evening of drinking.

chef_bio.background: A small, unpretentious late-night ramen counter tucked into the Nagarekawa-Yakkenbori nightlife district of central Hiroshima, about 1.5km from the Peace Memorial Park. It draws a steady crowd of locals looking for a warming bowl to close out an evening of drinking.
chef_bio.philosophy: Simple, comforting late-night food done well — the kind of straightforward bowl meant to satisfy after a night out.
chef_bio.specialty: An assari (light) soy-sauce chuka soba with thin noodles and a broth described as gently sweet and comforting, finished with carefully slow-simmered pork chashu. The shop is also known for its grilled shumai (焼シュウマイ), offered both steamed and grilled and available for takeout.

anecdotes.text: The shop reportedly once served a tonkotsu salt ramen but shifted its menu to the lighter soy-sauce chuka soba, a change a local food blogger linked to the COVID-19 period.
Regulars treat it as the classic after-drinking 'shime' (closing meal) spot, valued for its warm, no-frills atmosphere right in the heart of the entertainment quarter.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: ホットペッパーが薬研堀の中華そば店として、細麺の醤油スープ（濃厚なのにあっさり）、こだわりの豚チャーシュー、名物の焼シュウマイ（蒸しに対し焼き、テイクアウト可）を紹介。アメブロのブログは、以前の豚骨塩ラーメンからコロナ期に中華そば主体へ変えたこと、締めの一杯として甘みのある優しい味わいを伝える。

gf_cross_contamination.text: Kitchen is built around wheat ramen noodles, fried rice, and shumai; high likelihood of gluten cross-contact throughout. No gluten-free handling documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Broth is soy-sauce based; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Meat-based broth and pork chashu; karaage and pork shumai also prepared in the same small kitchen, so vegan-safe preparation is not feasible.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny late-night counter where ordering is simple but staff likely speak little English, so basic Japanese or pointing at the menu will make the visit smoother.

hiro_seichan.gf_detail: Gyoza are wrapped in wheat-flour skins (thin wheat wrappers), so neither the grilled nor the fried gyoza are gluten-free. The dipping/scallion sauce is also expected to contain wheat-based soy sauce. There are no gluten-free menu items.
hiro_seichan.vegan_detail: The entire menu is pork gyoza (twice-ground pork with chives and garlic) served with a scallion sauce, plus beer. There are no vegetable-only or vegan options, and the dipping sauce is not vegan-friendly.
hiro_seichan.hours_raw: Tue–Sat 17:00–21:00; closed Mon, Sun, and holidays
hiro_seichan.notes: [Mom & Pop] A tiny eight-seat counter gyoza shop tucked in Hiroshima's Nagarekawa entertainment district, in business for well over half a century (mid-1960s founding). It has long held a reputation as one of the city's most beloved and hardest-to-book gyoza counters.

chef_bio.background: A tiny eight-seat counter gyoza shop tucked in Hiroshima's Nagarekawa entertainment district, in business for over half a century (roughly 58 years, mid-1960s founding). It has long held a reputation as one of the city's most beloved and hardest-to-book gyoza counters.
chef_bio.philosophy: She runs the whole place herself and treats it as a warm gathering spot rather than just an eatery, carefully managing the limited counter so regulars and guests are looked after. As she puts it, the gyoza skins are alive, which makes the frying difficult, so each batch demands her full attention.
chef_bio.specialty: Pan-fried pork gyoza, made fresh each day. The proprietress arrives around 6:30 each morning to begin her preparations, using twice-ground pork mixed with chives from Kochi and garlic from Aomori, all wrapped in specially ordered thin skins. She steam-fries dozens of gyoza at once in a lard-coated iron pan, rotating it with practiced movements.

anecdotes.text: She celebrates customers' birthdays by setting candles on a plate of gyoza instead of a cake.

Gyoza arrive with a bean-sprout garnish and a scallion sauce; she playfully tucks extra scallions and sprouts into the dumpling folds, calling it the scallion pocket. Diners are sent off with a complimentary azuki (red-bean) ice bar once they finish.
She arrives at the shop around 6:30 every morning to begin the day's preparations before service.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: BRUTUSの記事が、女将・千鶴子さんが一人で切り盛りする8席のカウンター餃子店（創業約58年）で、朝6時半から仕込み、二度挽きの豚肉に高知のニラ・青森のニンニクを合わせ特注の薄皮で包むこと、ラードをひいた鉄鍋で焼くこと、『皮は生きているので焼くのが難しい』という言葉、もやしとねぎダレ・“ねぎポケット”の遊び、締めの小豆アイスバーを紹介している。

gf_cross_contamination.text: The only dishes are wheat-flour-skinned gyoza, prepared in a single shared lard-coated iron pan, so a single-item wheat kitchen offers no gluten-free path and high cross-contact.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Gyoza are served with a scallion-based dipping sauce; like standard Japanese gyoza sauce this is expected to be soy-sauce based (wheat-containing). Not independently confirmed as wheat-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All gyoza are pork-filled and the kitchen handles only pork gyoza, so there is no vegan preparation and unavoidable animal-product contact.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny eight-seat counter run single-handedly by an elderly proprietress with no English and reservations strongly advised, so some Japanese (or a Japanese-speaking companion) and patience will make the visit far smoother.

hiro_chuka_ryori_ryuoh.gf_detail: This is a standard Chinese stir-fry and ramen kitchen: dishes are seasoned with wheat-based soy sauce, the spring rolls and ramen are wheat, and there is no gluten-free menu or accommodation documented. Not suitable for strict gluten-free diners.
hiro_chuka_ryori_ryuoh.vegan_detail: The kitchen centers on meat dishes — liver-and-chive stir-fry (ニラ肝炒め), char siu pork ramen, and meat spring rolls — and uses wheat soy sauce and likely animal-based broths. No vegan or vegetarian options are documented.
hiro_chuka_ryori_ryuoh.hours_raw: Mon–Sat 17:00–03:00 next day (L.O. 02:50); Sun and holidays 17:00–02:30 next day (sources vary: official site lists Sun/holidays 17:00–02:00 next day, L.O. 01:50). Closed Mon (with occasional irregular closures).
hiro_chuka_ryori_ryuoh.notes: [Mom & Pop] A long-standing neighborhood Chinese eatery tucked into Hiroshima's Yakenbori nightlife district, near the Gomachi and Ginzan-cho streetcar stops and a short walk from the Peace Memorial Park area. It keeps the kitchen open into the small hours, making it a familiar lat

chef_bio.background: A neighborhood Chinese eatery in Hiroshima's Yakenbori nightlife district (near the Gomachi and Ginzan-cho streetcar stops, about a five-minute walk). It keeps the kitchen open into the small hours (until around 3am), making it a familiar late-night stop for locals winding down an evening out.
chef_bio.specialty: Home-style, no-frills neighborhood Chinese (machi-chuka) — set meals, single à-la-carte plates, and noodle, rice and soup dishes — the kind of comforting cooking a familiar local Chinese shop is known for, with ramen the house is noted for having a clean, pleasant aftertaste.
chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 公式サイト・gorpのメニューページ・ヒトサラが、龍王を薬研堀（1-13、胡町・銀山町電停から徒歩約5分）の“広島なじみの中華屋さん”とし、定食・一品料理・麺飯類を提供、月〜土17:00〜翌3:00の深夜営業、ラーメンは後味が良いと紹介する。具体的な個別メニュー名は各ソースで確認できなかったため一般化した。

gf_cross_contamination.text: Standard Chinese kitchen frying spring rolls and serving wheat ramen alongside stir-fries; shared woks and fryers make cross-contact with wheat highly likely.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes are seasoned in the typical machi-chuka style with soy sauce, which in Japan is wheat-based unless stated otherwise.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Menu is built around meat (liver, char siu pork, meat spring rolls) cooked on shared equipment; no vegan preparation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A late-night local Chinese diner where the menu and service are in Japanese, so some basic Japanese or a translation app helps, but pointing at dishes works fine.

hiro_taishu_gyoza_club_gyomuc.gf_detail: A gyoza-focused izakaya. Gyoza wrappers are made of wheat flour, so the signature dishes are not gluten-free, and dipping sauces are standard soy-sauce-based (wheat-containing). There is no documented gluten-free menu, no dedicated fryer, and no published allergen handling. Not suitable for strict gluten-free diners.
hiro_taishu_gyoza_club_gyomuc.vegan_detail: The menu centers on meat gyoza (pork with garlic) and izakaya fare such as Taiwanese fried chicken. No vegan or vegetarian menu is documented; fillings and broths use meat, and standard soy sauce is used. Not a vegan-friendly destination.
